p.src: Now Bajie leapt down the mountain and found a narrow path. Following it for some five or six li, he suddenly saw two female demons drawing water at a well. How did he know they were demons? Each wore atop her head a plaited-bamboo chignon fully a foot and two or three inches high—a style quite out of fashion. The fool went up to them and called, “Demons!” At this the two creatures flew into a rage and said to each other, “What an insolent monk! We have never met him, nor have we ever traded familiar banter with him. How dare he call us demons?” Enraged, they swung up the carrying pole and struck him squarely on the head.

p.src: The fool had no weapon in hand and could not ward off the blows. After taking several hits, he fled back up the mountain clutching his head and cried, “Brother, let’s turn back! Those demons are vicious.” “How are they vicious?” asked Pilgrim. Bajie said, “Two female demons were drawing water from a well in the hollow. I merely called out to them once, and they struck me three or four times with their pole.” Pilgrim asked, “What did you call them?” Bajie replied, “I called them demons.” Pilgrim laughed. “Then you got off lightly.” “Much obliged for your concern,” said Bajie. “My head is swollen from the beating, and you still call that light!” Pilgrim said, “With gentleness one may travel anywhere beneath Heaven; with stubborn force one cannot advance an inch. They are monsters of this place, while we are monks from afar. Even if your whole body were hands, you should still show a little courtesy. You went and called them demons outright. If they did not beat you, were they to beat me instead? Courtesy and propriety must come first in dealing with others.” Bajie said, “Now I understand even less.” Pilgrim said, “You have eaten people in the mountains since childhood, but do you know the two kinds of wood?” “No,” said Bajie. “What kinds of wood?” Pilgrim said, “One is poplar, and the other is sandalwood. Poplar is soft by nature. When a skilled craftsman obtains it, he may carve a holy image or a likeness of the Tathagata, gilding and painting it, inlaying it with jade and decorating it with flowers. Myriads burn incense and bow before it, and it receives immeasurable blessings. Sandalwood, however, is hard and unyielding. The oil press takes it and makes it into a pressing wedge; its head is bound with iron hoops and hammered down with an iron mallet. It suffers all this solely because it is so hard.” Bajie said, “Brother, you should have told me these wise words earlier. Then I would not have taken that beating.” Pilgrim said, “Go back and find out the truth from them.” Bajie said, “If I go back now, they will recognize me.” “Transform yourself before you go,” said Pilgrim. Bajie said, “Brother, even if I transform myself, how am I to question them?” Pilgrim said, “Go in another form, bow when you reach them, and judge how old they are. If they are about our age, call them ‘young ladies’; if they are somewhat older, call them ‘grannies.’” Bajie laughed. “What wretched luck! So far from home, how am I supposed to recognize such relatives?” Pilgrim said, “You are not claiming kinship; you are trying to draw them into conversation. If they have taken Master, we shall know where to strike; if they have not, then would we not be delaying our business elsewhere?” Bajie said, “That makes sense. Wait here while I go again.”

p.src: The good fool tucked his muckrake into his belt, descended into the hollow, shook himself, and transformed into a plump, dark-complexioned monk. Swaying from side to side, he approached the demons, made a profound bow, and said, “Grannies, this humble monk pays his respects.” The two were delighted. “Now this is a fine monk! He knows how to bow properly and address us with respect.” They asked, “Venerable sir, where have you come from?” “Where have I come from?” replied Bajie. They asked again, “Where are you going?” Again he replied, “Where am I going?” They asked once more, “What is your name?” Again he answered, “What is my name?” The demons laughed. “This monk is pleasant enough, but he has no story of his own and merely parrots whatever we say.” Bajie asked, “Grannies, why are you drawing water?” One demon replied, “Monk, you do not know. Tonight our old mistress seized a Tang monk and brought him into the cave. She means to entertain him, but the water in our cave is unclean, so she sent the two of us here to draw this excellent water where yin and yang mingle. We are to prepare a vegetarian banquet of fruits and vegetables for the Tang monk; after he has eaten, she will marry him tonight.”

p.src: On hearing this, the fool hastily slipped away and ran back up the mountain, shouting, “Brother Sha, bring the luggage quickly! Let us divide it among ourselves.” “Second Brother,” said Sha Monk, “why divide it again?” Bajie said, “Once it is divided, you can return to the Flowing Sands River and eat people, I can visit my kin at Gao Old Manor, Elder Brother can go back to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit and proclaim himself a sage, and the White Dragon Horse can return to the sea and become a dragon. Master is already going to marry in the demon’s cave, so let each of us go and find his own livelihood.” Pilgrim said, “This fool is talking nonsense again.” Bajie retorted, “Your son is talking nonsense! Those two water-carrying demons just said they were preparing a vegetarian banquet for the Tang Monk, after which he is to be married.” Pilgrim said, “The demon has imprisoned Master in her cave, and he is anxiously waiting for us to rescue him, yet here you are saying such things.” Bajie asked, “How are we to rescue him?” Pilgrim said, “You two lead the horse and carry the luggage. We shall follow those two female demons and use them as guides. Once they lead us to the entrance, we shall all strike together.”

p.src: The fool had no choice but to go along. Pilgrim kept the two demons in sight from afar. They gradually entered the deep mountains and went some ten or twenty li, when suddenly the women vanished. Bajie exclaimed in alarm, “Master was taken by daylight ghosts!” Pilgrim said, “What keen eyes you have! How did you see through to their true forms?” Bajie replied, “Those two creatures were carrying water, then suddenly vanished. If they are not daylight ghosts, what are they?” Pilgrim said, “They must have slipped into their cave. Wait here while I take a look.”

p.src: The Great Sage quickly opened his Fiery Eyes and Golden Pupils and searched the whole mountain, but indeed saw no sign of movement. Before a steep cliff, however, he saw an exquisitely wrought ceremonial arch, delicately adorned with flowers, heaped with five-colored ornament, and crowned by three tiers of clustered eaves. He went closer with Bajie and Sha Monk to inspect it. Across the top were six large characters: “Bottomless Cave of Hollow-Trap Mountain.” Pilgrim said, “Brothers, the fiend has set up this grand front here, but we still do not know where its door opens.” Sha Monk said, “It cannot be far. Let us search carefully.” When they all turned to look, they saw beneath the arch, at the foot of the mountain, a great slab of rock more than ten li across. Right in its center was a hole as wide as the mouth of a vat, its sides worn glassy smooth by crawling passage. Bajie said, “Brother, this must be the cave through which the fiend comes and goes.” After looking at it, Pilgrim said, “How strange! Ever since I, Old Monkey, began protecting the Tang Monk—and I have no need to hide it from you two—we have met and captured quite a few fiends, but never have I seen a lair like this. Bajie, you go down first and test how deep it is, so that I may enter and rescue Master.” Bajie shook his head. “That is difficult—far too difficult. This old hog of yours has such a hulking body that if my footing gave way and I fell, who knows whether I would reach the bottom in two or three years?” Pilgrim said, “Can it truly be that deep?” Bajie said, “Look for yourself.” The Great Sage lay prone beside the opening and peered carefully downward. Ah! How deep it was—and fully three hundred li around. He turned back and said, “Brother, it truly is exceedingly deep.” Bajie said, “Then you had better turn back. Master cannot be saved.” Pilgrim said, “What sort of talk is that? Do not give way to laziness or let negligence enter your heart. Set down the luggage for now and tether the horse to a pillar of the arch. You wield your rake, and Sha Monk his staff, and guard the mouth of the cave while I go inside to investigate. If Master truly is inside, I shall drive the fiend out with my iron staff. When it flees to the entrance, you two must bar its way from outside: thus we shall strike from within and without. Only by killing the fiend can we rescue Master.” The two obeyed his command.

p.src: Pilgrim sprang into the air and leaped down into the cave; ten thousand rays of colored cloud formed beneath his feet, while a thousand folds of auspicious vapor guarded his body. Before long he reached its remote depths, where all was bright and clear: there was sunlight as elsewhere, the sound of wind, and flowers, grasses, fruit trees, and other trees besides. Pilgrim rejoiced. “What a splendid place! When I, Old Monkey, came into the world, Heaven bestowed the Water-Curtain Cave upon me; this place too is a blessed grotto, a paradise of its own.” As he looked, he saw another gatehouse with a double-drip roof, encircled by pines and bamboo, with many buildings within. He thought again, “This must be the fiend’s dwelling. I shall go inside and make some inquiries. Wait. If I go in like this, she will recognize me. I had better transform myself before I go.” He shook himself, formed the spell with his fingers, and changed into a little fly, which gently alighted atop the gatehouse to listen. He saw the fiend seated high in a thatched pavilion. She looked quite different from when he had rescued her in the pine forest and seized her in the monastery, for she had made herself more beautiful than ever:

p.src: Pilgrim remained silent for the moment and listened to what she would say. Presently she parted her cherry lips and called out delightedly, “Servants, quickly lay out a vegetarian banquet! Brother Tang Monk and I shall eat, then be married.” Pilgrim laughed inwardly. “So it is true! I thought Bajie was merely joking and talking nonsense. Let me fly inside and search for Master to see where he is. I wonder how steadfast his heart may be? If by chance she has fondled and tempted him into yielding, I may as well leave him here.” He spread his wings and flew farther inside. There, beneath the eastern gallery, behind a red-paper lattice bright above and dark below, sat the Tang Monk.

p.src: Pilgrim butted through one of the lattice holes, flew onto the Tang Monk’s bald head, settled there, and called, “Master.” Tripitaka recognized his voice and cried, “Disciple, save my life!” Pilgrim said, “Master, you are hopeless! That fiend is preparing a banquet so that she may eat with you and then marry you. If you happen to beget a son or daughter, there will even be descendants of you, a monk. What have you to worry about?” Hearing this, the elder gnashed his teeth and said, “Disciple, ever since I left Chang’an and took you as my disciple at the Mountain of Two Frontiers, as we have journeyed westward, at what moment have I ever broken my abstinence? On what day have I ever harbored an improper thought? Now this fiend has captured me and demands that I become her mate. If I lose my true yang, I shall fall into the cycle of rebirth, be cast behind the Dark Mountain, and never in all eternity rise again.” Pilgrim laughed. “Do not swear such oaths. Since you are sincere in your resolve to fetch the scriptures from the Western Heaven, I, Old Monkey, shall take you away.” Tripitaka said, “I have completely forgotten the way by which we entered.” Pilgrim said, “Never mind that you have forgotten it. This cave is not one that you simply walk into and out of; one must bore downward from above. Once I rescue you, we shall have to bore upward from the bottom. If our fortune is high and we strike the opening, we shall get out; but if our fortune is low and we miss it, there will come a day when we suffocate to death.” With tears filling his eyes, Tripitaka said, “With matters so difficult, what are we to do?” Pilgrim said, “It is all right, it is all right. The fiend is preparing wine for you to drink. You have no choice, so drink one cup of it. Only have her pour it briskly enough to raise a festive blossom of foam; I shall change into a tiny insect and fly beneath the bubbles. When she swallows me in one gulp, I shall tear apart her heart and liver, wrench her guts asunder, and kill the fiend; only then will you be able to escape.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, to do as you say would be most inhumane.” Pilgrim said, “Go on practicing nothing but mercy and your life will be finished. That fiend is the very root of harm to humankind. Why pity her?” Tripitaka said, “Very well, very well. Only be sure to stay with me.” Indeed:

p.src: Before master and disciple had finished their discussion, the fiend had already completed her preparations. She came outside the eastern gallery, unlocked and opened the door, and called, “Elder.” The Tang Monk dared not answer. She called once more, and again he dared not answer. Why did he dare not respond? He was thinking, “When the mouth opens, the vital spirit scatters; when the tongue moves, disputes arise.” Yet another thought occupied his mind: “If I remain obstinately silent, I fear she may harden her heart and take my life in an instant.” Truly, caught between advance and retreat, his heart questioned his mouth; pondering thrice and enduring, his mouth questioned his heart. While he still wavered, the fiend called once more, “Elder.” The Tang Monk had no choice but to answer, “My lady, I am here.” When the elder forced out those words, it was truly as though a thousand-jin weight of flesh had fallen from him. Everyone says that the Tang Monk was a monk of true resolve who journeyed to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures; why, then, did he answer this female fiend? They do not understand that at this moment his life hung in the balance and he had no choice whatsoever. Though outwardly he gave an answer, inwardly he harbored no desire. When the fiend heard the elder answer, she pushed open the door, helped the Tang Monk to his feet, and went with him hand in hand, shoulder pressed to shoulder, their heads close together as she whispered in his ear. Just look at the thousand coquettish poses and ten thousand amorous charms she displayed. Little did she know that Tripitaka’s whole heart was filled with distress. Pilgrim laughed secretly. “With Master being coaxed and enticed by her in this fashion, I fear his heart may waver for a moment.” Indeed:

p.src: The demoness extended her slender jade fingers and raised a gleaming golden cup. Filling it to the brim with fine wine, she offered it to the Tang Monk and called sweetly, “Dear Elder, my wonderful man, please drink this cup of nuptial wine.” Tripitaka bashfully accepted the wine and poured a libation toward the sky, praying silently, “All you guardian devas, the Five Directional Messengers, and the Duty Gods of the Four Watches: I, your disciple Chen Xuanzang, have journeyed from the Eastern Land. By the Bodhisattva Guanyin’s command, you gods have secretly protected me as I go to worship at Thunderclap Monastery, behold the Buddha, and seek the scriptures. Now, on the road, I have been captured by a demoness who is forcing me to marry her and has handed me this cup of wine to drink. If this truly is vegetarian wine, may your disciple drink it under compulsion and still behold the Buddha and accomplish his mission; but if it is strong wine, and your disciple’s precepts are thereby broken, may she fall forever into the torments of rebirth.” The Great Sage Sun had transformed himself into something tiny and nimble, like a whispering familiar behind Tripitaka’s ear; when he spoke, only Tripitaka could hear him, and no one else. Knowing that his master ordinarily enjoyed vegetarian wine made from grapes, he told him to drink a cup. With no other choice, the master drank it, then quickly filled a cup to the brim and returned it to the demoness. Sure enough, a festive blossom formed on the surface as he poured. Pilgrim transformed himself into a tiny insect and gently flew beneath the festive blossom. The demoness took the cup but did not drink at once. She set it down, bowed twice with the Tang Monk, and coyly murmured several words of love. Only then did she raise the cup, but the blossom had already dispersed, exposing the insect. The demoness did not recognize it as Pilgrim’s transformation and took it for an ordinary bug. She lifted it on her little finger and flicked it away.

p.src: He sprang into the air, swept out his jade talons, and with a great crash overturned the banquet table. Vegetarian fruits and dishes, plates, bowls, pots, and goblets were all smashed to pieces; then, leaving the Tang Monk behind, he flew away. The demoness was so terrified that her heart and gall nearly split, while the Tang Monk too felt his flesh and bones turn to jelly. Trembling all over, the demoness clung to the Tang Monk and said, “Dear Elder, where did that creature come from?” Tripitaka replied, “This poor monk does not know.” The demoness said, “I took such pains to arrange this vegetarian feast so that you and I might enjoy ourselves, yet who knows where that feathered beast flew in from and smashed all my household ware?” The lesser demons said, “My lady, the broken household ware matters little, but all the vegetarian delicacies have been spilled on the ground and defiled. How can we use them now?” Tripitaka knew perfectly well that this was Pilgrim’s magic, but how would he dare say so? The demoness said, “Little ones, now I understand. It must be that Heaven and Earth cannot tolerate my holding the Tang Monk captive, and so sent down this creature. Carry out the broken ware and prepare more wine and food, whether meat or vegetarian. I shall call Heaven to witness as matchmaker and Earth as witness to our betrothal, and then I shall marry the Tang Monk.” As before, she had the elder escorted to the eastern gallery and seated there; of this, no more for now.

p.src: Now Pilgrim, having flown outside, resumed his true form, went to the mouth of the cave, and called, “Open the door!” Eight Rules laughed and said, “Brother Sha, our elder brother is back.” The two of them moved their weapons aside. Pilgrim leaped out, and Eight Rules stepped forward, caught hold of him, and asked, “Is there a demoness inside? Is Master there?” Pilgrim said, “Yes, yes, yes.” Eight Rules asked, “Is Master suffering in there? Is he tied up or bound fast? Are they going to steam him or boil him?” Pilgrim replied, “Nothing of that sort. She has only prepared a vegetarian feast and means to do that business with him.” Eight Rules said, “Lucky you, lucky you! Have you been drinking the wedding attendants’ wine?” Pilgrim said, “You idiot! Master’s life can scarcely be saved, so what wedding wine would I be drinking?” Eight Rules asked, “Then why have you come back already?” Pilgrim related the whole story of how he had seen the Tang Monk and used his transformations. Then he said, “Brothers, cease your wild imaginings. Master is certainly here. This time I go in, I shall surely rescue him.”

p.src: He turned and went back inside, transformed once more into a fly, and alighted on the gate tower to listen. He heard the demoness, still fuming with anger, order from the pavilion, “Little ones, bring meat or vegetarian food—it matters not—and prepare offerings to burn. We shall trouble Heaven and Earth to serve as matchmaker and witness, for I am determined to marry him.” Hearing this, Pilgrim laughed inwardly and thought, “This demoness has not the least sense of shame. In broad daylight she has shut a monk in her house to do with as she pleases. But there is no need to hurry. Let old Sun go in and look once more.” With a buzz, he flew beneath the eastern gallery and saw his master sitting inside, clear tears streaming down his cheeks. Pilgrim slipped inside, alighted on his head, and called again, “Master.” Recognizing his voice, the elder sprang up and said through clenched teeth, “You macaque! When other people are bold, their bodies still contain their courage; but your courage is so great that it contains your entire body. What good did it do to employ your transformations and magic merely to smash her household ware? You have only stirred that demoness’s lust to a fever. Now she cares nothing for meat or vegetarian fare and is determined to couple with me. How is this to be resolved?” Pilgrim gave an ingratiating laugh from his hiding place and said, “Do not blame me, Master. I have a way to save you.” The Tang Monk asked, “How can you save me?” Pilgrim replied, “When I flew up just now, I saw a flower garden behind this place. Coax her into going there with you for amusement, and I shall rescue you.” The Tang Monk asked, “How will you save me in the garden?” Pilgrim said, “When you enter the garden with her, stop when you reach the peach trees. I shall fly onto a peach branch and transform myself into a red peach. When you ask to eat some fruit, choose the red one and pluck it first. The red one will be me. She will surely want to pick one too, and you must insist on yielding the red one to her. If she swallows me in one bite, I shall be inside her belly. Then I will smash her skin sack, tear apart her liver and guts, and kill her, and you will be free.” Tripitaka said, “If you have such abilities, why not simply challenge her to battle? Why must you crawl into her belly?” Pilgrim replied, “Master, you do not understand the situation. If this cave were easy to enter and leave, I could indeed fight her; but its entrances and exits are awkward and its winding passages difficult to traverse. If I start fighting here, her entire nestful, old and young alike, will seize even me. What would we do then? Only by doing it this sudden, underhanded way can we all make a clean escape.” Tripitaka nodded and accepted his plan, saying only, “Stay close to me.” Pilgrim replied, “I understand, I understand. I am right here on your head.”

p.src: Once master and disciples had settled their plan, Tripitaka slowly rose, grasped the lattice with both hands, and called, “My lady, my lady.” Hearing him, the fiend ran up with a beaming smile and said, “My darling brother, what is it you wish to say?” Tripitaka said, “My lady, ever since I left Chang’an and journeyed westward, not a day has passed without mountains or rivers. Yesterday I lodged at Sea-Calming Monastery, where I happened to contract a severe chill. I perspired today and have only just begun to recover. Then, through your great kindness, I was brought into your immortal abode. But after sitting here all day, I once again feel out of sorts. Would you take me somewhere to stroll a little, clear my mind, and enjoy myself?” The fiend was delighted. “My darling brother is in a playful mood after all. Let us go and amuse ourselves in the garden.” She called, “Servants, bring the key, open the garden gate, and sweep the paths.” The lesser fiends all ran off to open the gate and put the place in order.

p.src: The elder walked through the garden with the monster, admiring an inexhaustible profusion of rare blossoms and strange plants. They passed many pavilions and galleries, and truly the scenery grew lovelier at every step. Suddenly he looked up and found that they had reached the edge of a peach grove. Monkey pinched his master on the head, and the elder immediately understood. Monkey flew onto a branch of a peach tree, shook himself, and changed into a red peach, beautifully crimson indeed. The elder said to the fiend, “My lady, the flowers in your garden are fragrant and the fruit upon the branches is ripe. Bees vie to gather from the fragrant garden flowers, and birds contend to peck the ripe fruit on the boughs. Why, then, are the peaches on this tree not all the same, some green and some red?” The fiend laughed. “Without yin and yang in Heaven, the sun and moon would not shine; without yin and yang on Earth, plants and trees would not grow; without yin and yang among humankind, there would be no distinction between male and female. As for the fruit on this peach tree, those peaches facing the sun are warmed by its rays and ripen first, which is why they are red; those on the shaded side, where the sun does not reach, remain unripe and are therefore green. Such is the principle of yin and yang.” Tripitaka said, “Thank you for instructing me, my lady. I truly did not know.” He immediately reached forward and plucked a red peach. The fiend also went and plucked a green peach. Bowing, Tripitaka presented the red peach to the monster and said, “My lady, since you delight in bright colors, please eat this red peach and give me the green one.” The fiend actually exchanged peaches with him and secretly rejoiced: “What a fine monk! We have not yet been husband and wife for even a day, yet already he shows me such affection.” Overjoyed, the fiend treated the Tang Monk with tender affection. The Tang Monk took the green peach and began to eat it. The fiend happily kept him company, opened her mouth, and was about to bite the red peach. She parted her vermilion lips and revealed her pearly teeth, but before she could bite down, Sun Wukong, ever impatient, somersaulted straight down her throat and went directly into her belly. Terrified, the fiend said to Tripitaka, “Elder, that fruit was formidable! How did it roll down before I even had a chance to bite it?” Tripitaka said, “My lady, fruit from a newly opened garden is eager to be eaten, so it went down quickly.” The fiend said, “I had not even spat out the stone before it darted down.” Tripitaka said, “My lady, your gracious feelings made you so eager to eat it that it went down before you had time to spit out the stone.”

p.src: When Monkey heard her from inside, he feared that the elder’s compassionate heart might let her deceive him again. So he swung his fists, kicked his feet, set himself firmly, and struck in all directions, almost battering a hole through that sack of skin. Unable to endure the pain, the fiend collapsed in the dust and for a long while could not utter a word. When she said nothing, Monkey thought she might be dead and relaxed his hands a little. She caught her breath again and called, “Where are my servants?” As it happened, after entering the garden, the lesser fiends had tactfully scattered. Some picked flowers, others played games with plants, and all amused themselves as they pleased, leaving the fiend and the Tang Monk alone to speak freely of love. Only when they suddenly heard her call did they all come running back. Seeing the fiend lying on the ground, her face discolored, groaning and unable to rise, they hurriedly helped her up, gathered around, and asked, “Madam, what is wrong? Has your heart ailment suddenly flared up?” The fiend said, “No, no. Do not ask questions. There is already a man inside my belly. Quickly carry this monk outside and save my life.” The lesser fiends actually came forward to lift and carry him. From inside her belly, Monkey shouted, “Who dares carry him? You must personally offer up my master and take him outside. Once we are out, I shall spare your life.” The monster had no choice, for she cherished her life. She struggled hastily to her feet, put the Tang Monk on her back, strode off, and headed outside. The lesser fiends followed and asked, “Old Madam, where are you going?” The fiend replied, “So long as the bright moon remains above the five lakes, why worry that there will be nowhere else to cast a golden hook? Let me send this fellow away, and I shall find another mate later.”
